extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (metaphysics/epistemology); scholars interested in perception, causality, and the principle of sufficient reason
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the nature of perception, the role of the understanding and reason, the principle of sufficient reason, and related distinctions (subject/object, reality/dream, illusion). Forms the first book of a philosophical treatment of the world as idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception presupposes the law of causality (a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: All perception — that is to say all experience — depends upon the law of causality, and the knowledge of causality is a priori; causality does not arise from experience but is its condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues this deduction by showing perception is 'pure knowledge through the understanding of the cause from the effect' and cites perceptual phenomena (children learning to see, stereoscope, double vision) as evidence that the understanding includes causality prior to experience. It is offered as a refutation of Hume's scepticism that causality is derived from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception is intellectual (understanding infers cause from effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception is not merely sensory data; it is intellectual — 'pure knowledge through the understanding of the cause from the effect' — by which the understanding converts raw sensations into perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: development of sight in children and operated blind persons, single vision from two eyes, stereoscope, upright perception despite inverted retinal image. The understanding's one simple function transforms 'dull, meaningless sensation into perception' by passing from effect to cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse subject–object relation with cause–effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation of subject and object is not a relation of cause and effect; applying the principle of sufficient reason to subject–object leads to confusions about the reality of the outer world (realism vs idealism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns this is a grave error that produced disputes between dogmatism and scepticism. It argues that subject and object precede knowledge and are outside the province where the principle of sufficient reason applies; hence one cannot prove realism or idealism by treating subject/object as cause/effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-as-idea and empirical reality (transcendental ideality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceived world in space and time is entirely real as idea (empirical reality) yet is determined by the subject (transcendental ideality); demanding an object existing outside idea is meaningless and contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes empirical reality (the world as it appears, bound by causality) from the metaphysical demand for an 'object in itself' independent of subject. It asserts the reality of perceived objects consists in their causal action and that 'knowledge of the nature of the effect of any perceived object exhausts such an object itself, so far as it is object.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Different forms of the principle of sufficient reason — being vs knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of sufficient reason takes different forms: for abstract concepts (knowing) it demands a ground of knowledge; for real objects (being) it functions as the law of causality, a ground of being — these forms must not be confused or misapplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying the principle of sufficient reason of knowing to perceived objects is a category error. The text explains that among concepts the principle links judgments to grounds of knowledge; among real objects it appears as causality: every real object 'has paid its debt' by coming to be as effect of a cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for distinguishing dreams from reality: causal continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's suggested criterion: the connection of ideas according to the law of causality constitutes the difference between real life and dreams — i.e., long-life has overarching causal continuity that individual short dreams lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes Kant's criterion is of limited practical use because we cannot trace every causal chain; the empirical criterion of awaking (which breaks causal connection) is more reliable. The text acknowledges difficulties and that sometimes it remains uncertain whether an event was dreamt or real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body as immediate object; form known indirectly via understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The body is the starting-point and immediate object for the subject because bodily changes supply the first data; nevertheless the body's form (as an object in space) is not known by mere feeling but only through the understanding's application of causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man born blind gains form from touch gradually; a blind man without hands could not construct his form. The text stresses that sensation precedes understanding but that objecthood (extended form) arises only after understanding infers relations among bodily parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding versus reason: immediate intuition vs abstract concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding is the faculty that immediately infers cause from effect (shared by animals), whereas reason forms abstract concepts and general rules; reason makes immediate insights permanent but does not itself produce immediate perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical discoveries (Hooke, Newton, Lavoisier, Goethe) are presented as examples of understanding's apperçu (flash of insight) — immediate inferences from effects to causes — with reason later formalizing these insights into abstract laws. Understanding is prior for perception and discovery; reason is reflective and discursive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusion arises when the same effect admits two possible causes and the understanding defaults to the commoner cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Illusion (deception of the understanding) occurs when the same effect may be attributed to two causes, one frequent and one rare; lacking further data the understanding assumes the common cause and perceives a false object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: double sight from displaced organs, stick appearing broken in water, reflections in curved mirrors, apparent enlargement of the moon at the horizon. The text emphasizes that such illusions are immediate perceptions and often persist despite abstract explanation from reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology tying cognitive deficiencies to faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific cognitive deficiencies are labelled: 'stupidity' = deficiency of understanding (dulness in applying causality); 'foolishness' = deficiency in applying reason to practice; 'silliness' = deficiency of judgment; 'madness' = partial/entire deficiency of memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay gives behavioral illustrations (e.g., an imbecile boy fascinated by reflections as example of lack of understanding) and explains that these terms denote different lacking faculties rather than a single generic failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding is present a priori in animals; distinguish understanding from instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: All animals possess understanding sufficient to infer from effects on the immediate object to indirectly known causes (hence are animals); understanding exists a priori in animals, while instinct is a distinct faculty that may resemble combined understanding and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: animals display varying degrees of sagacity (elephant refusing unsafe bridge; orangutan failing to keep a found fire alight indicates absence of abstract deliberation). The distinction between understanding and instinct is deferred to later discussion but is asserted as important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological starting-point: start from the idea (form of subject/object) not subject or object alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical method should start from the idea (which presupposes both subject and object) and consider subordinate forms (time, space, causality) as forms of the object that can nonetheless be known a priori from the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method contrasts with previous systems that start either from object or subject and try to explain one from the other. The principle of sufficient reason is thus confined to the object, not extended improperly to the subject.
